hypothesis: Selecting the strongest visible verifier result across all fresh attempts will outperform submitting the first candidate that passes visible tests.
Continuing each failed attempt from its candidate code while repairing reported verifier failures will outperform restarting from pristine code with the same feedback.
One candidate-based repair followed by a fresh, failure-informed restart will improve resolved rate by combining targeted repair with a final chance to escape a failing patch.

For tasks with no fully passing candidate, repairing the strongest partially passing candidate will increase the visible-pass rate by preserving behavior that already passes while fixing remaining failures.

For tasks whose initial candidate passes all visible checks, an independent review and repair from that candidate will reduce visible-pass hidden-fail outcomes by catching gaps beyond the visible checks.

For tasks whose first high-effort candidate fails visible checks, a medium-effort independent second attempt followed by a configured-effort final attempt will improve the never-visible-pass rate by adding reasoning diversity while retaining a strong last attempt.
Aggregating failures and regressions across fresh retries will help later attempts resolve never-visible-pass tasks by exposing recurring verifier problems that last-attempt-only feedback can hide.

For never-visible-pass tasks, repair the strongest candidate only when it passes at least one visible check and restart from fresh after zero-pass attempts, because partial success is useful evidence about which behavior to preserve while zero-pass patches provide a poor repair base.

A dedicated plan-only call for tasks that do not reach a visible pass, persisted in a temporary repository-root file for the implementation call, will reduce task interpretation and approach errors enough to raise resolved rate despite consuming one of the three agent calls.

For tasks that do not reach a visible pass, use the first call to reproduce the reported behavior before fixing it, so a concrete failing check guides the implementation and reduces symptom-only patches.

For tasks whose first candidate passes zero visible checks, a low-effort fresh second attempt followed by a configured-effort final attempt will improve the never-visible-pass rate by introducing a simpler independent approach while preserving a strong final retry.

For tasks that never pass all visible checks, continue from the latest candidate only when its visible pass count strictly exceeds every earlier attempt; this preserves demonstrated progress while fresh retries escape stagnating or regressing patches.

For tasks without a visible pass, contrasting only the two latest verifier runs by persistent failures, new regressions, and recovered checks will guide fresh retries better than last-run-only feedback by showing both unresolved behavior and what improved.

For tasks whose first verifier run reports an execution error, one repair call from that candidate before fresh retries may raise the never-visible-pass rate because the code context supports fixing a localized execution defect.

For never-visible-pass tasks, starting at medium effort and escalating failed retries to the configured high effort may improve visible-pass rate by producing a more direct initial solution while retaining stronger recovery attempts.

For tasks that never pass visible checks, continue from the latest candidate only when its visible pass count strictly exceeds every earlier candidate; this uses demonstrated progress as a repair base while fresh retries escape stagnation, revisiting an invalid unmeasured experiment.

For tasks that never visibly pass, adding the strongest prior candidate's passing check names as preservation targets to each fresh retry may reduce regressions while the latest verifier failures guide the fix.

For never-visible-pass tasks, continue from the latest candidate only when it passes a visible check no earlier candidate passed, so equal-score complementary progress can be repaired without continuing candidates that repeat or regress known coverage.

For tasks that first pass visible checks only after a failed attempt, auditing that passing candidate from its code may catch feedback-induced overfitting and improve hidden-test generalization while retaining the original pass as a fallback.

For tasks that never pass visible checks, repair the strongest candidate only when it passes a majority of visible tests; broad passing coverage signals a coherent approach worth completing, while lower coverage favors a fresh attempt.

For never-visible-pass tasks, keep the first two retries independent and repair the strongest candidate on the final call only when it passed a visible check, preserving demonstrated behavior while using earlier calls for diversity.
